scenario_stem:
Silverbirch Aerospace Plc is a public limited company in Country X that manufactures small aircraft components, employing 240 workers and reporting revenue of $18 million last year. The company now wants to build a new $6.5 million production plant to meet rising orders from overseas customers and cut delivery times from 14 days to 10 days.

The Board is deciding between two external sources of finance. Option 1 is to issue 2.5 million new shares on the Country X stock exchange at $2.60 each. Option 2 is a bank loan of $6.5 million over 8 years at a fixed interest rate of 8.5% per year, costing $552,500 in interest every year. The Finance Director warns that the loan would add heavy fixed repayments, while existing shareholders own 40 million shares and fear control of the company would be diluted if new shares are issued.

questions.question_text: Define 'issue of shares' as a source of finance.
questions.model_answer: An issue of shares is the sale of shares (small ownership stakes) in a company to investors in exchange for capital. It is a long-term source of external finance available to limited companies, and the money raised does not have to be repaid. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Sale of shares (ownership stakes) to investors for capital
Money raised does not have to be repaid; long-term external finance for limited companies

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of issuing new shares rather than taking a bank loan to finance the new plant.
questions.model_answer: First advantage: issuing shares provides the $6.5 million of capital without adding fixed repayments, so $552,500 a year of interest is saved and cash flow is eased while the 240 workers are paid [k], which suits a company whose revenue is already $18 million and whose overseas orders are rising [app]. Second advantage: shares carry no obligation to repay the capital, unlike the 8-year bank loan at 8.5%, so the risk of insolvency is reduced if profits fall [k], and the $2.60 issue price means 2.5 million new shares raise exactly the $6.5 million needed without increasing the company's debt [app].

knowledge_max_2: No repayment obligation and no interest to pay on share capital
Reduces insolvency risk compared with fixed loan repayments
application_max_2: $6.5 million raised matches the cost of the new plant
$552,500 per year of interest avoided
2.5 million shares at $2.60 equals $6.5 million

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of issuing new shares for the existing shareholders of Silverbirch Aerospace Plc.
questions.model_answer: First disadvantage: existing shareholders' ownership would be diluted, because issuing 2.5 million shares to new investors reduces the percentage held by the owners of the existing 40 million shares [k], meaning each share receives a smaller slice of any future dividends and has weaker voting power over how the new $6.5 million plant is run [app], so existing investors may resist the issue or demand a higher share price [an]. Second disadvantage: control of the company could change hands, because new shareholders voting at the AGM may outvote current holders on key decisions [k], for example whether the $6.5 million raised is reinvested to cut delivery times or paid out as dividends [app], so the original owners risk losing their ability to steer the company's long-term strategy [an].

knowledge_max_2: Dilution of existing shareholders' ownership percentage
Possible loss of control; weaker voting power over decisions
application_max_2: 2.5 million new shares compared with existing 40 million shares
Dividend per share and voting strength reduced for current holders
Decisions on spending the $6.5 million / cutting delivery times
analysis_max_2: Dilution leads to smaller dividends and weaker influence, causing shareholder resistance
Loss of control means original owners cannot direct company strategy

questions.question_text: Do you think Silverbirch Aerospace Plc should issue new shares rather than take the 8-year bank loan to finance the new plant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Issuing shares would raise the full $6.5 million needed for the plant without creating fixed repayments, saving $552,500 a year of interest and keeping cash flow healthy while orders grow [k], and because revenue is already $18 million with 240 workers, the company can afford to dilute the 40 million existing shares by issuing 2.5 million new ones at $2.60 [app], so the business avoids the risk of defaulting on the loan if overseas demand weakens [an]. However, the bank loan would keep ownership and control unchanged and protect the existing 40 million shares from dilution, costing only $552,500 per year of interest, which a business with $18 million revenue could comfortably cover [k], and loan interest is tax-deductible whereas share dividends are not, and unlike share issues the loan does not permanently reduce shareholders' claim on profits [app], so the loan is less damaging to owners in the long run [an]. Overall, I think the company should issue the new shares, because eliminating $552,500 of annual interest and avoiding 8 years of fixed repayments outweighs the dilution from a 2.5 million share issue when the plant will cut delivery times and win more overseas orders [eval]. The decision would change only if the current owners refused any loss of control, in which case the bank loan would be the safer choice [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Share issue raises capital without repayment; loan adds fixed repayments and interest
Loan preserves existing ownership and control; interest is tax-deductible
application_max_2: $6.5 million required matches both options
$552,500 annual interest vs $18 million revenue and 240 workers
2.5 million new shares at $2.60 vs existing 40 million shares
analysis_max_2: No fixed repayments reduce default risk during demand fluctuations
Dilution reduces owners' claim on profits and control
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation weighing interest saving against dilution
Acknowledges the alternative view/conditions under which the choice would change

scenario_stem:
Bramblehurst Joinery Co is a private limited company in Country X that makes bespoke fitted kitchens and bedroom furniture, employing 45 workers across a workshop and a showroom. Revenue last year was $3.2 million and profit was $290,000. The business needs $850,000 to buy a CNC routing machine so that cutting times fall from 9 days to 4 days per kitchen.

The two founding families own all the shares and are deciding between two external sources of finance. Option 1 is a bank loan of $850,000 over 5 years at 9% interest, costing $76,500 per year and $382,500 in total interest. Option 2 is to issue new shares worth $850,000 to the two founding families, who would then own 60% of the company instead of 75%. Option 1 keeps ownership unchanged but adds fixed annual repayments; Option 2 brings in cash with no interest but dilutes control.

questions.question_text: Define 'bank loan' as a source of finance.
questions.model_answer: A bank loan is a sum of money borrowed from a bank or other lender for an agreed period, to be repaid with interest in instalments. It is a long-term external source of finance commonly used to purchase fixed assets such as machinery. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Borrowing from a bank or lender for an agreed period
Repaid with interest, usually in regular instalments

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the bank loan may be attractive to Bramblehurst Joinery Co.
questions.model_answer: First reason: the loan provides the full $850,000 needed to buy the CNC routing machine without giving up any ownership, because the two founding families keep their shares and control the business [k], which matters to them since Option 2 would cut their holding from 75% to 60% [app]. Second reason: although the $76,500 annual interest is a fixed cost, the machine should cut cutting times from 9 days to 4 days per kitchen and win more orders, lifting revenue above $3.2 million so the interest is comfortably covered [k], and the 5-year term spreads repayment instead of demanding one large up-front sum the business cannot fund from profit of $290,000 alone [app].

knowledge_max_2: Large sum available immediately without losing ownership
Repayments spread over an agreed period; control retained by owners
application_max_2: $850,000 needed for the CNC routing machine
$76,500 per year interest versus $290,000 profit
Cutting time reduced from 9 days to 4 days per kitchen

questions.question_text: Explain two risks of taking the bank loan rather than issuing shares to the founding families.
questions.model_answer: First risk: the loan creates fixed repayments of about $76,500 per year plus principal for 5 years, regardless of profits [k], so if revenue falls below $3.2 million or a major kitchen contract is lost, the business could fail to pay and the bank could demand repayment or seize the CNC routing machine offered as security [app], meaning the business faces a real risk of insolvency during a downturn [an]. Second risk: interest of $382,500 over the 5 years is a direct cost that reduces net profit [k], so profit of $290,000 last year would drop sharply once interest is paid, leaving little retained profit for dividends or expansion [app], which limits the business's ability to fund future growth from internal sources [an].

knowledge_max_2: Fixed repayments must be made regardless of profit; default risk
Interest is a direct cost that reduces net profit and retained profit
application_max_2: $76,500 per year for 5 years plus $382,500 total interest
Profit of $290,000 would be heavily reduced by interest
CNC routing machine may be used as security
analysis_max_2: Fixed repayments in a downturn lead to insolvency risk
Higher interest charges leave less retained profit for future expansion

questions.question_text: Do you think Bramblehurst Joinery Co should take the bank loan rather than issue shares to the founding families? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Taking the bank loan keeps the founding families in complete control, with their holding at 75% instead of falling to 60% [k], and it provides the $850,000 for the CNC routing machine immediately so cutting times fall from 9 days to 4 days per kitchen and orders can rise [app], meaning the loan could pay for itself from extra revenue within a few years [an]. However, the loan adds fixed repayments of $76,500 a year plus interest totalling $382,500, which is heavy compared with profit of $290,000 last year [k], so a bad year could push the business into cash-flow difficulty, whereas issuing shares to the families would bring cash with no interest and no repayment deadline [app], although dilution to 60% would weaken the families' control over the business [an]. Overall, I think the business should take the bank loan, because keeping 100% family control and the prospect of faster production and higher revenue outweigh the $76,500 annual interest, provided the families are confident orders will grow [eval]. If sales were likely to fall, the share issue would be the safer option because it carries no repayment obligation [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Loan keeps ownership/control unchanged; shares dilute existing holders
Loan adds fixed repayments and interest; shares carry no repayment obligation
application_max_2: Holding stays at 75% versus 60% under share issue
$76,500 per year and $382,500 total interest versus $290,000 profit
$850,000 needed for CNC routing machine; cutting time 9 days to 4 days
analysis_max_2: Loan could pay for itself through faster production and more orders
Fixed repayments create cash-flow risk in bad years versus dilution risk of shares
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation supported by stem figures
Acknowledges conditions under which the decision would change

scenario_stem:
Ashwick Garments Ltd is a private limited company in Country X producing school uniforms for retail chains, employing 110 workers. Annual credit sales are $2.4 million and customers usually take 75 days to pay. At present $480,000 is owed by debtors, and the business is struggling to pay its own suppliers on time.

The Managing Director is choosing between two external sources of finance. Option 1 is to use a factoring company, which would advance 85% of the outstanding debts immediately, giving $408,000, and charges a fee of 3% of invoice value, about $14,400 a year. Option 2 is a bank loan of $350,000 over 3 years at 10% interest, costing $35,000 per year and $105,000 in total. Option 1 releases cash quickly but is more expensive; Option 2 is cheaper long term but adds a fixed monthly repayment.

questions.question_text: Define 'factoring of debts' as a source of finance.
questions.model_answer: Factoring of debts is when a business sells its outstanding customer invoices (debtors) to a specialist factoring company for immediate cash, usually at a discount. It is a short-term external source of finance that improves cash flow without waiting for customers to pay. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Selling outstanding invoices/debts to a factoring company
Cash received immediately, usually at a discount; improves cash flow

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of factoring the $480,000 of debts rather than taking the bank loan.
questions.model_answer: First advantage: factoring would release $408,000 immediately (85% of the $480,000 owed) [k], so the business can pay its suppliers on time and avoid running short of cash while customers take 75 days to settle [app]. Second advantage: the factor takes on the task of chasing and collecting payment from debtors [k], saving management time and letting the 110 workers focus on producing uniforms rather than debt collection [app].

knowledge_max_2: Immediate access to cash tied up in debtors; improves liquidity
Factor handles credit control/collection, releasing management time
application_max_2: Customers take 75 days to pay
Credit sales of $2.4 million per year

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of factoring the $480,000 of debts.
questions.model_answer: First disadvantage: factoring is expensive, with a fee of 3% of invoice value, about $14,400 a year, plus the 15% discount on the $480,000 of debts [k], so the business keeps only $408,000 of what it is owed, reducing profit from $2.4 million of credit sales [app], and this cost persists year after year while the factoring arrangement continues [an]. Second disadvantage: customers know their debt has been sold to a factor and may resent being chased by a third party [k], which could damage relationships with the uniform-chain buyers who place regular large orders [app], risking lost contracts and weakening Ashwick's reputation as a reliable supplier [an].

knowledge_max_2: Factoring is costly; fees and discounts reduce income received
Customer relationships and goodwill may be damaged by third-party collection
application_max_2: 3% fee = about $14,400 per year
Receives $408,000 of $480,000 owed (15% discount)
Uniform-chain buyers place regular orders
analysis_max_2: Ongoing fees reduce profit year after year
Strained customer relationships lead to lost orders and weaker goodwill

questions.question_text: Do you think Ashwick Garments Ltd should use factoring rather than a bank loan to solve its cash-flow problem? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Factoring would give the business $408,000 immediately without adding loan repayments, and the fee of about $14,400 a year is lower than the bank loan's $35,000 annual interest [k], and it would cover the gap created by customers taking 75 days to pay on $2.4 million of credit sales [app], relieving cash flow within weeks rather than after a lengthy loan application [an]. However, factoring costs 3% of every invoice ($14,400 a year) plus the 15% discount on the $480,000 debts, so over 3 years the total fees would exceed the $105,000 interest on a $350,000 bank loan [k], and the factor's control over debt collection could harm relationships with uniform-chain buyers who currently wait 75 days [app], which may matter more than the short-term saving on interest [an]. Overall, I think Ashwick should use factoring for its short-term cash-flow problem because the speed and lower annual cost outweigh the fee, provided customer relationships survive the handover to the factor [eval]. If the debt problem is long term, the bank loan at 10% would be cheaper over 3 years ($105,000) and would keep debt collection in-house [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Factoring provides immediate cash but charges fees and a discount
Bank loan adds fixed interest and repayments but is cheaper long term
application_max_2: $408,000 received immediately vs $350,000 loan option
$14,400 fee per year vs $35,000 interest per year and $105,000 total
Customers take 75 days to pay; $2.4 million credit sales
analysis_max_2: Factoring acts within weeks, closing the gap created by slow payers
Cumulative fees exceed loan interest over 3 years; collection handover harms relationships
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation weighing speed and cost against fees

scenario_stem:
Aldermoor Engineering Ltd is a private limited company in Country X producing precision metal castings for export, employing 320 workers with revenue of $24 million last year. The business needs $10 million to build a new export finishing facility and double overseas sales from 15% to 30% of output.

The Board is weighing two external-finance routes. Option 1 is to convert into a public limited company and issue new shares to the general public at $5.00 each, raising $10 million from 2 million shares, with listing costs of $400,000. Option 2 is to remain a private limited company and take a 7-year bank loan at 8% interest, costing $800,000 per year and $5.6 million in total interest. The twelve existing family shareholders fear losing control and their 80% combined holding if new public shares are issued.

questions.question_text: Define 'share capital' as a source of finance.
questions.model_answer: Share capital is the money raised by a company through the issue of shares to shareholders, who become part-owners of the company. It is shown in the statement of financial position and is a long-term source of finance for limited companies. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Money raised by issuing shares to shareholders
Shareholders become part-owners; shown in statement of financial position

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of converting to a Plc and issuing shares rather than taking the bank loan.
questions.model_answer: First advantage: issuing 2 million shares at $5.00 each raises the full $10 million needed for the export finishing facility without creating any repayment obligation [k], so unlike the 7-year bank loan costing $800,000 per year ($5.6 million in total), the company keeps more cash to fund the plan to double overseas sales from 15% to 30% of output [app]. Second advantage: a public listing raises the company's profile and makes future share issues and borrowing easier and cheaper [k], and the $400,000 listing cost is a one-off fee, far smaller than $5.6 million of interest over 7 years [app].

knowledge_max_2: Share capital need not be repaid; no interest is payable
Public listing raises profile and eases future fundraising
application_max_2: 2 million shares at $5.00 raises $10 million
$5.6 million total interest avoided ($800,000 per year)
$400,000 one-off listing cost compared with $5.6 million interest

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of issuing public shares for Aldermoor Engineering and its family shareholders.
questions.model_answer: First disadvantage: the existing twelve family shareholders fear losing control, since selling 2 million new shares to the public could reduce the family's combined 80% holding below 50% [k], giving outside investors power to influence decisions on the new export finishing facility and on dividends [app], so the founding family could lose the final say over the company's direction just as overseas sales are set to double [an]. Second disadvantage: public companies face much heavier legal and reporting duties, including publishing audited accounts and informing the stock exchange [k], costing time and about $400,000 just to list, money a 320-worker company could otherwise spend on the $10 million facility [app], reducing the finance actually available for the expansion [an].

knowledge_max_2: Dilution of family control; possible loss of majority ownership
Heavier legal disclosure and reporting requirements for public companies
application_max_2: Family's 80% combined holding could fall below 50%
$400,000 listing cost reduces funds for the $10 million facility
320 workers depending on export expansion
analysis_max_2: Loss of control means outside investors steer strategy at a critical moment
Listing and disclosure costs reduce capital available for the expansion

questions.question_text: Do you think Aldermoor Engineering should convert to a public limited company and issue shares rather than remain private and take the bank loan? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Converting to a Plc would raise the $10 million needed through 2 million shares at $5.00 each, with no interest to pay and no $800,000 annual charge for 7 years ($5.6 million saved) [k], and the issue would give the family easier access to large sums of capital for its plan to double overseas sales from 15% to 30% of output [app], removing the fixed repayment burden that a $24 million-revenue private company must carry even in weak trading years [an]. However, selling public shares could cut the family's 80% holding below 50%, so they would lose control of the company they built [k], and public status brings audit costs, listing fees of about $400,000 and ongoing disclosure duties that a 320-worker private limited company has so far avoided [app], which may outweigh the interest saving if the family values control above growth [an]. Overall, I think Aldermoor should remain a private limited company and take the 7-year bank loan, because preserving 80% family control and avoiding the disclosure burden matters more than saving $5.6 million of interest, provided profits can cover the $800,000 annual interest [eval]. If the family wanted to grow faster and share the risk with outside investors, the public share issue would be the bolder and cheaper long-term choice [eval].

Public status brings disclosure duties; loan keeps company private and control intact
application_max_2: 2 million shares at $5.00 raises $10 million; $5.6 million interest avoided
Family's 80% holding could fall below 50%
$400,000 listing cost and disclosure burden for a 320-worker business
analysis_max_2: No fixed repayments protect cash flow in weak trading years
Loss of majority control gives outside investors influence over strategy
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation weighing control against interest savings
Acknowledges conditions under which the public issue would be preferable

scenario_stem:
Mwangaza Weavers Co-operative is a small handloom weaving enterprise in Country X employing 18 artisan weavers. Members have saved $9,000 between them and sales reached $210,000 last year. The co-operative wants $45,000 to buy two new looms and train six members in modern weaving designs, which would lift output from 120 to 180 pieces a month.

The members are comparing two external sources of finance. Option 1 is a micro-finance loan of $45,000 from a rural micro-finance institution at 12% interest over 3 years, costing $5,400 per year and $16,200 in total interest. Option 2 is a rewards-based crowdfunding campaign aiming to raise $45,000 from online backers, with the platform charging a 6% fee and a target that may not be met. Micro-finance offers a guaranteed sum but adds fixed repayments; crowdfunding costs nothing if it fails but could leave the looms unbought.

questions.question_text: Define 'micro-finance' as a source of finance.
questions.model_answer: Micro-finance is the provision of very small loans and other financial services to small businesses or individuals who cannot access traditional bank finance. It is usually delivered by specialist local institutions and supports micro-enterprises and start-ups. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Very small loans provided to those excluded from bank finance
Provided by specialist local institutions to micro-enterprises or start-ups

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of micro-finance for Mwangaza Weavers Co-operative.
questions.model_answer: First advantage: micro-finance guarantees the full $45,000 the co-operative needs for the two new looms and training [k], unlike the crowdfunding option whose target may never be met [app]. Second advantage: the micro-finance institution specialises in rural enterprises and can offer financial advice and support [k], helping 18 artisan weavers run the co-operative professionally as output rises from 120 to 180 pieces a month [app].

knowledge_max_2: Guaranteed access to the required funds if approved
Tailored to small/rural enterprises, often with business advice and support
application_max_2: $45,000 needed for two looms and training
Output to rise from 120 to 180 pieces a month
Members' savings of $9,000 are insufficient alone

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of micro-finance for Mwangaza Weavers Co-operative.
questions.model_answer: First disadvantage: the micro-finance loan adds fixed repayments of $5,400 of interest per year for 3 years ($16,200 in total) [k], which is heavy for a business with sales of only $210,000 and members' savings of $9,000 [app], so a fall in orders could put the looms and the co-operative's future at risk [an]. Second disadvantage: $45,000 is still a small sum, so Mwangaza cannot use micro-finance to fund much larger expansion or exporting later [k], meaning that if the two looms succeed and output reaches 180 pieces a month, the co-operative will soon outgrow this source of finance [app], limiting its ability to scale up production [an].

knowledge_max_2: Interest and repayments burden small cash flows
Micro-finance provides only small sums, limiting expansion scope
application_max_2: $5,400 per year interest; $16,200 in total over 3 years
Sales of $210,000 and members' savings of $9,000
Output limited until looms arrive
analysis_max_2: Weak cash flow raises default and insolvency risk
Outgrowing the source forces refinancing and constrains growth

questions.question_text: Do you think Mwangaza Weavers Co-operative should use micro-finance rather than crowdfunding to raise the $45,000? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Micro-finance guarantees the $45,000 needed for the two looms and skills training, with a predictable cost of $5,400 of interest per year ($16,200 over 3 years) [k], so the 18 artisan weavers can plan output rising from 120 to 180 pieces a month with confidence [app], removing the risk of a crowdfunding campaign that might fail and leave the looms unbought [an]. However, crowdfunding would let the co-operative raise the $45,000 without any debt or interest, and with only a 6% platform fee it would be cheaper than $16,200 of interest [k], and a successful online campaign would also test demand and build a backer community who could become loyal customers of handmade woven products [app], turning the fundraising itself into free marketing [an]. Overall, I think Mwangaza should use micro-finance, because the guaranteed $45,000 and predictable repayments matter most to an 18-member rural co-operative that cannot afford a failed campaign [eval]. If the members are confident of reaching the $45,000 online target, crowdfunding would be cheaper and would build useful marketing buzz [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Micro-finance: guaranteed sum but fixed repayments and interest
Crowdfunding: no debt, only a platform fee, but target may not be met
application_max_2: $45,000 required for looms and training; 6% platform fee vs $16,200 interest
Output rising from 120 to 180 pieces a month
18 artisan weavers and members' savings of only $9,000
analysis_max_2: Guaranteed funds allow confident production planning
Crowdfunding provides marketing value and demand testing alongside funding
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation weighing certainty against cost and marketing
Acknowledges when crowdfunding would be the better choice

scenario_stem:
Solway Green Energy Ltd is a private limited company in Country X installing commercial solar systems for farms and factories, employing 65 workers. Last year revenue was $7.8 million. The company needs $1.2 million to buy battery-storage equipment so it can store surplus power and offer clients a full day-and-night service.

The Board is considering two external-finance routes. Option 1 is to accept a government subsidy covering 30% of the equipment cost, $360,000, on condition that 60% of parts are sourced locally and progress is reported for 5 years; the remaining $840,000 would come from a bank loan at 7.5% over 6 years, costing $63,000 per year. Option 2 is a bank loan for the full $1.2 million at 7.5% over 6 years, costing $90,000 per year and $540,000 in total interest. Option 1 saves interest but brings conditions and paperwork; Option 2 is flexible but dearer.

questions.question_text: Define 'subsidy' as a source of finance.
questions.model_answer: A subsidy is a payment or financial support given by the government to a business to encourage the production of certain goods and services. It reduces the business's costs and is a form of long-term external finance. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Payment or financial support from the government to a business

Second advantage: a government subsidy signals official support and strengthens Solway's reputation with farms and factories [k], potentially helping win more of the commercial solar contracts behind its $7.8 million revenue [app].

Second disadvantage: subsidies are often slow to approve and can be withdrawn or changed by future governments [k], so if the 60% local-sourcing condition cannot be met or approval is delayed, the company may miss the installation season when farms want a day-and-night service [app], leaving the $1.2 million equipment order unfunded and the expansion stalled [an].

If local sourcing proves impossible or much costlier, the single larger bank loan would be the more practical route [eval].

scenario_stem:
Drummond Alloys Ltd is a well-established private limited company in Country X producing copper and aluminium alloys, employing 150 workers with revenue of $9 million last year. A new $2 million furnace is needed to replace ageing plant that breaks down about 12 times a year.

The Finance Manager has drawn up two external options. Option 1 is a bank loan of $2 million over 5 years at 8% interest, costing $160,000 per year in interest. Option 2 is to issue a $2 million debenture at 7.5% interest, redeemable after 10 years, with the debenture holders having no ownership but first claim on assets if the company fails.
